doc.title: Hal Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: Growing up in the Dixieland revival instead of rock and roll
summary: Born in 1953, he loved ragtime and banjo music of the Dixieland revival and heard the Firehouse Five at Disneyland at eight, wanting trombone until braces.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: How come you didn’t go the rock & roll route?

When I was a kid I was growing up at the very end of the Dixieland revival, started by Lu Watters and Turk Murphy, including Bunk Johnson, Kid Ory. And the second wave of that was honky tonk piano and banjo, barber shop quartets. That was real popular when I was a kid, all over the radio, on the T.V.
Because we’re similar in age, I’m a little older than you, but I was not aware that there was a revival of Dixieland at all.

Well it was more pronounced in California. That was the hot bed of it, the Bay area, and Los Angeles to a lesser degree. But the bands that made it big, banjo bands or pianos to have a hit single, Crazy Otto, Johnny Maddox, Joe “Fingers” Carr, people like that, you could hear those things on the radio very easily and there were lots of recordings of “Waiting for the Robert E. Lee,” “Alabama Jubilee,” things like that. I mean, I could walk into any record store in Indianapolis and find those things.

So it was just kind of a happy music, and it wasn’t a protest music like rock & roll. I heard Elvis Presley, I remember Bill Haley and the Comets and all that, it just never did anything for me. And I like ragtime and the banjo music and all that kind of thing, and that’s what led me into an appreciation of Dixieland, when I finally, I heard the Firehouse Five at Disneyland, when we moved to California when I was eight. I was taken to Disneyland for my birthday, the first live jazz band I ever heard, that’s it. That wiped out everything I’d heard before.
And you were playing at that time, which instrument were you playing?

I was not settled on anything. I’d gone from piano to banjo — I was playing clarinet, just reading out of the exercise book at that point. And I heard that and the trombone got my imagination, and I really wanted to play that but then the braces came.
